title: Foreign Keys and Table Relationships
learningObjectives: Explain the core concepts of Foreign Keys and Table Relationships.
Identify the SQL structures and terminology used in this topic.
Read and interpret an original SQL example related to Foreign Keys and Table Relationships.
Predict the expected behaviour or result of a query in the stated engine context.
Apply safe and maintainable practices when using this concept.

understand.concept: A foreign key is a constraint that links one or more columns in a child table to a candidate key, usually the primary key, in a parent table. It helps enforce referential integrity by preventing references to missing parent rows, subject to the configured database rules.
understand.whyItMatters: Foreign keys model relationships between entities and protect data consistency. For example, an order can refer to an existing customer rather than storing an unverified customer identifier.
understand.analogy: A foreign key is like a reference number on a form that must match an existing entry in a master register.
understand.analogyLimit: A reference number alone does not guarantee that the related record exists; the database must enforce the foreign-key constraint. Enforcement settings and syntax can vary by DBMS.

explain.narrative:
## Parent and child tables
A parent table contains the referenced key. A child table contains the foreign key. For example, Customer(customer_id) can be the parent and Orders(customer_id) the child. Each order refers to a customer.

## Referential integrity
A foreign key can prevent a child row from referring to a parent key that does not exist. It can also define what happens when a referenced parent row is updated or deleted, using actions such as RESTRICT, CASCADE or SET NULL where supported and appropriate.

## SQLite enforcement
SQLite supports foreign-key constraints, but enforcement must be enabled for each connection using PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON. A browser Playground must initialize this setting for every database connection/session. Other database engines have their own defaults and configuration rules.

## Relationship types
One-to-many is commonly represented by placing the foreign key on the many side. Many-to-many relationships generally use a junction table containing foreign keys to both parent tables. One-to-one relationships require an additional uniqueness rule on the foreign-key column.

## Design carefully
Choose matching compatible key types, index foreign-key columns when useful for workload and understand delete/update actions before using CASCADE. Do not use cascading deletion without considering the business meaning and recovery requirements.

examples.title: Create parent and child tables
examples.expectedOutput: Tables created; foreign-key enforcement enabled for this connection
examples.explanation: SQLite requires foreign-key enforcement to be enabled per connection. The child table references the parent primary key.

examples.title: Insert a parent then a child
examples.code:
INSERT INTO Customer VALUES (1, 'Asha');
INSERT INTO Orders VALUES (501, 1);
examples.expectedOutput: 1 row inserted into Customer; 1 row inserted into Orders
examples.explanation: The referenced customer exists before the order is inserted.

examples.title: Join child rows to their parent
examples.code: SELECT Orders.order_id, Customer.name FROM Orders JOIN Customer ON Orders.customer_id = Customer.customer_id;
examples.explanation: The join matches the foreign-key value to the parent key.

examples.title: Reject an orphan reference
examples.explanation: With SQLite foreign-key enforcement enabled, a child row cannot reference a missing customer. Exact error text varies.

examples.title: Model a many-to-many relationship
examples.code:
CREATE TABLE Course (course_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, title TEXT NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE Enrollment (student_id INTEGER, course_id INTEGER, PRIMARY KEY (student_id, course_id), FOREIGN KEY (course_id) REFERENCES Course(course_id));
examples.explanation: A junction table stores associations. A production Enrollment table would also reference a Student primary key; the example focuses on the course-side relationship and composite identity.

practise.guidedTask: Study the five examples for Foreign Keys and Table Relationships. For each example, identify the SQL statement, predict its effect or result, then verify it in a compatible SQL engine when available.
practise.independentTask: Create a small relational database scenario that demonstrates Foreign Keys and Table Relationships. Write at least three queries or statements, explain the expected result, and identify any assumptions about the database dialect.

questions.prompt: Which table normally contains the referenced key in a foreign-key relationship?
questions.explanation: The parent table exposes the referenced candidate key, commonly its primary key.

questions.prompt: What does a foreign key help enforce?
questions.explanation: A foreign key can prevent child rows from referencing missing parent rows.

questions.prompt: In SQLite, what must be enabled on a connection for foreign-key enforcement?
questions.explanation: SQLite foreign-key enforcement must be enabled for each connection.

questions.prompt: Where is a foreign key commonly placed for a one-to-many relationship?
questions.explanation: Each child row stores the key of its related parent row.

questions.prompt: How is a many-to-many relationship commonly represented?
options: With a junction table that references both related tables
By duplicating all columns into one table
By using a single nullable text field
questions.answer: With a junction table that references both related tables
questions.explanation: A junction table stores associations and normally contains foreign keys to both parent tables.
